problems.title: Finite entropy does not establish strict positivity
problems.source_location: Appendix A, Lemma A.4, proof of the Gibbs optimizer; Theorem A.5
claim: The proof states that an optimizer must have positive density because otherwise its entropy objective is infinite, then uses multiplicative variations to derive an Euler equation over the domain.
analysis: On \([0,1]\), density \(p=2\) on the first half and zero elsewhere has finite entropy \(\int p\log p=\log2\), using \(0\log0=0\). It is not the optimizer; it disproves the finiteness rationale rather than the optimizer formula. Multiplicative variations preserve its zero set, so a separate full-support argument is needed. If “positive density” means only absolute continuity, the existence-of-density statement is reasonable but still does not justify strict positivity in the later variation step.
result: The lemma’s conclusion remains valid under its stated bounded-continuous residual and positive-temperature assumptions; the proof needs completion, not a reversed theorem verdict.
repair: For bounded continuous \(f_0\), let \(Z=\int e^{f_0/\beta}\), \(q=e^{f_0/\beta}/Z\). Then \(E(p)=\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)-\beta\log Z\), proving the unique optimizer \(q\), including full support. At unit domain volume and residual sup norm \(a_n\to0\), \(0\le\beta\log Z_n\le a_n\) and \(p_n\to1\) uniformly.

problems.title: The boundary penalty changes with shared ball geometry
problems.source_location: Eqs.(8)–(10),(13), main algorithm; boundary-term independence statement near the geometry update
claim: The same centers/radii parameterize normalized expert gates and the adaptive density. Fixed boundary coordinates do not make predictions at those coordinates independent of geometry.
analysis: On \([0,1]\), use constant experts \(U_1=0,U_2=1\), centers \(0,1\), radii \(2,2\), endpoint boundary targets zero and the printed quartic gates. Every endpoint lies strictly inside both balls. Predictions are \(u(0)=9/25,u(1)=16/25\), hence mean boundary loss \(B=0.2696\). Differentiating only the second radius gives \(\partial_{s_2}u(0)=96/625\), \(\partial_{s_2}u(1)=0\), and \(\partial_{s_2}B=864/15625=0.055296\ne0\). Thus dropping the term is not the full tied-geometry gradient. Freezing the ansatz during a density-only surrogate update, exact boundary enforcement or zero residual can legitimately remove it, but fixed sample coordinates alone cannot.
result: The written omission needs a declared detachment/surrogate policy or the missing derivative. Without author implementation, historical computational-graph behavior and numerical impact remain unknown.
repair: For the full tied geometry, include \(\nabla_\varphi B\) and both the direct residual derivative and density derivative in the interior term. A frozen-proposal importance estimator must hold its samples/denominator fixed while differentiating the numerator. Alternatively explicitly define a density-only frozen-ansatz surrogate and analyze that method separately.
